findings.explanation:
Two requirements, two interfaces, and they are doing different jobs. Database.Batchable carries the volume; Schedulable supplies the recurrence. The Schedulable class's execute() calls Database.executeBatch() on the Batchable class, and System.schedule() sets it to run after hours.
Queueable loses the volume slot on the query. A queueable job is a single transaction with a single set of governor limits, and the limit on total records retrieved by SOQL queries is 50,000 in asynchronous Apex exactly as it is in synchronous Apex — so being async buys nothing, and selecting every Contact in an org of more than 50,000 fails outright. Heap tells the same story: 12 MB in async, which 50,000 Contact records will not fit inside. Batch Apex escapes this by a documented mechanism rather than by being bigger: if start() returns a Database.QueryLocator, the governor limit for the total number of records retrieved by SOQL queries is bypassed, and a QueryLocator can cover up to 50 million records. Separately, each execute() chunk is a discrete transaction whose governor limits are reset, which is what gives the processing room. Those are two different guarantees, and only Batch Apex offers either.
Queueable can't take the other slot either, which is the likelier place to go wrong on a choose-two. The requirement is a recurring time of day — once a day, after business hours — and a queueable has no vocabulary for that. Its only timing control is System.enqueueJob(queueable, delay), where the delay is a minimum of 0 to 10 minutes and is ignored entirely during Apex testing. There is no recurrence and no time of day in it. Schedulable is the interface that takes a cron expression, through System.schedule() or the Schedule Apex page, and the Apex Scheduler documentation names this pairing directly: it is "ideal for daily or weekly maintenance tasks using Batch Apex".
The @future annotation is the weakest option: it can't be scheduled, returns no job id, can't be chained, and accepts only primitives and collections of primitives as arguments. The 50 usually quoted alongside @future is the maximum number of future methods allowed per Apex invocation — a cap on how many future calls one transaction can make, not a cap on records per call.
One detail that catches people out: scheduled Apex is asynchronous, but synchronous governor limits apply to a scheduled job. Schedulable on its own therefore buys no headroom, which is exactly why the Batchable half of this answer is required and not merely tidier.
